title: Erdős Problem #1072: Least n with n! ≡ −1 (mod p)
description: For prime p, let f(p) be the least n with n! + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p). By Wilson's theorem, f(p) ≤ p-1. Are there infinitely many p with f(p) = p-1? Is f(p)/p → 0 for almost all p? Status: OPEN.

meta.author: Erdős–Hardy–Subbarao
meta.assumptions: 3 axiom declarations (all OPEN conjectures): erdos_1072a (infinitely many maximal primes), erdos_1072b (f(p)/p → 0 for almost all primes), hardy_subbarao_belief (maximal primes have density 0). All provable axioms eliminated: wilson_theorem, f_le_pred, f_pos, f_of_2, f_of_3, f_of_5, f_of_7, f_of_11, f_of_13. Wilson-maximality decided explicitly on {2,3,5,7,11,13}: maximal {2,3,5,13}; non-maximal {7,11}.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős, Hardy, and Subbarao posed this problem in their 2002 American Mathematical Monthly paper on problems involving factorials. The question builds directly on Wilson's theorem—proved by Lagrange in 1771 and named after John Wilson—which guarantees that $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$ for every prime $p$. The natural follow-up is: can this congruence be achieved earlier? The function $f(p) = \min\{n \geq 1 : n! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}\}$ measures how early the Wilson congruence first appears. Computational evidence (OEIS A154554) shows that $f(p)$ is often much smaller than $p-1$: for instance $f(7) = 3$ since $3! + 1 = 7$, and $f(23) = 14$. Hardy and Subbarao conjectured that Wilson-maximal primes (where $f(p) = p-1$) have density zero among all primes, paralleling the sparsity conjectures for twin primes and Wilson primes. The problem also connects to Guy's *Unsolved Problems in Number Theory* (Problem A2) and to the broader Erdős program of understanding the arithmetic of factorials. The question about Wilson primes—primes $p$ with $p^2 \mid (p-1)! + 1$—is a related but much harder condition; only three Wilson primes ($5, 13, 563$) are known despite searches to $5 \times 10^{17}$.
overview.problemStatement: For prime $p$, define $f(p) = \min\{n \geq 1 : n! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}\}$. (1) Are there infinitely many primes with $f(p) = p - 1$? (2) Does $f(p)/p \to 0$ for almost all primes?
overview.text: For prime p, let f(p) be the least n with n! + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p). By Wilson's theorem, f(p) ≤ p-1. Are there infinitely many p with f(p) = p-1? Is f(p)/p → 0 for almost all p? Status: OPEN.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization defines $f(p)$ via Lean's `sInf` on the set $\{n > 0 : p \mid n! + 1\}$, which is well-defined by Wilson's theorem. Wilson-maximality (`isWilsonMaximal`) captures $f(p) = p-1$. The upper bound $f(p) \leq p-1$ and lower bound $f(p) \geq 1$ (for $p \geq 3$) are axiomatized. Both main conjectures are stated as axioms, along with the Hardy-Subbarao density belief. Small examples ($f(2)=1, f(3)=2, f(5)=4, f(7)=3$) are recorded, and the relationship to Wilson primes is formalized: every Wilson prime is Wilson-maximal.
keyInsights: Wilson's theorem guarantees $f(p) \leq p-1$ for all primes, but the function $f(p)$ captures how far below this bound the first factorial hit occurs—the 'Wilson gap' $p - 1 - f(p)$ measures how much slack exists

The first non-maximal prime is $p = 7$ since $3! + 1 = 7$: the factorial sequence $1, 2, 6, 24, \ldots$ modulo 7 hits $-1 \equiv 6$ at $n = 3$ before the guaranteed $n = 6$. This is because $7$ is a factorial prime ($n! + 1 = p$), a very special coincidence

The Hardy-Subbarao conjecture that maximal primes have density zero is analogous to the twin prime conjecture: both assert that a naturally defined subset of primes is sparse but possibly infinite. No theoretical progress exists for either direction of Problem #1072

Wilson primes ($p^2 \mid (p-1)! + 1$) are a strictly stronger condition than Wilson-maximality. Only $5, 13, 563$ are known. If there are infinitely many Wilson primes, that would give infinitely many Wilson-maximal primes—but the converse fails dramatically

The function $f(p)$ connects to the multiplicative structure of $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$: the sequence $1!, 2!, \ldots, (p-2)!$ modulo $p$ traces a path through the cyclic group, and $f(p) = p-1$ means this path avoids $-1$ until the final step forced by Wilson's theorem

Heuristically, if factorial residues modulo $p$ behaved like random elements of $\{1, \ldots, p-1\}$, the probability of maximality would be $(1 - 1/(p-1))^{p-2} \to e^{-1} \approx 0.37$—suggesting positive density, contradicting the Hardy-Subbarao conjecture. The discrepancy highlights hidden structure in factorial residue sequences

sections.title: Module Docstring
sections.summary: States Erdős Problem #1072: for a prime $p$, $f(p)$ is the least $n>0$ with $n!+1\equiv0\pmod p$ (i.e. $n!\equiv-1$). Wilson's theorem gives $f(p)\leq p-1$. Questions: (1) are there infinitely many primes with $f(p)=p-1$? (2) is $f(p)/p\to0$ for almost all primes? Status OPEN; belief: maximal primes have density 0 (OEIS A154554).

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.summary: Defines `leastFactorialWilson p` $=f(p)=\inf\{n>0:p\mid n!+1\}$ and `isWilsonMaximal p` ($p$ prime $\wedge f(p)=p-1$).

sections.title: Wilson's Theorem and Bounds
sections.summary: PROVES `wilson_theorem` ($p\mid(p-1)!+1$, from Mathlib's `ZMod.wilsons_lemma`), `f_le_pred` ($f(p)\leq p-1$), and `f_pos` ($f(p)\geq1$ for $p\geq3$).

sections.title: Question 1: Infinitely Many Maximal Primes
sections.summary: States the AXIOM `erdos_1072a` (OPEN): there are infinitely many primes $p$ with $f(p)=p-1$.

sections.title: Question 2: f(p)/p → 0 for Almost All Primes
sections.summary: States the AXIOM `erdos_1072b` (OPEN): there is a density-1 set of primes along which $f(p)/p\to0$.

sections.title: Hardy–Subbarao Belief
sections.summary: Provides a `DecidablePred isWilsonMaximal` instance and states the AXIOM `hardy_subbarao_belief` (OPEN): the count of $p\leq x$ with $f(p)=p-1$ is $o(x/\log x)$ (density 0 among primes).

sections.title: Small Examples
sections.summary: Computes $f$ on small primes by `sInf` + `decide`: `f_of_2` ($=1$), `f_of_3` ($=2$), `f_of_5` ($=4$), `f_of_7` ($=3<6$, first non-maximal), `f_of_11` ($=5$), `f_of_13` ($=12$).

sections.title: Known Wilson-Maximal Primes
sections.summary: PROVES the maximality classification: `isWilsonMaximal_2`, `_3`, `_5`, `_13` (maximal) and `isNotWilsonMaximal_7`, `_11` (not maximal) — isolating $7,11$ as the first non-maximal primes (OEIS A154554).

sections.title: Connection to Wilson Primes
sections.summary: A note: Wilson primes ($p^2\mid(p-1)!+1$, e.g. $5,13,563$) are empirically maximal, but this is not proved in general; the problem concerns $f(p)$, not the strength of the Wilson congruence.
sections.mathContext: Wilson primes ($p^2\mid(p-1)!+1$) empirically maximal, but unproven in general.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Closing docstring recapping the proved theorems (Wilson bound, $f$-values, maximality of $2,3,5,13$, non-maximality of $7,11$), the 3 remaining open axioms (erdos_1072a/b, hardy_subbarao_belief), and the empirical small-prime status matching OEIS A154554.
sections.mathContext: Recap: 15 proved theorems, 3 open axioms; small-prime maximality sporadic (matches A154554).

conclusion.summary: This formalization captures Erdős Problem #1072, an open problem about the least $n$ for which $n! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$. Wilson's theorem guarantees $f(p) \leq p-1$, and the two main questions ask whether $f(p) = p-1$ infinitely often and whether $f(p)/p \to 0$ for almost all primes. The formalization includes 241 lines of Lean 4 with clean definitions via `sInf`, computed small examples establishing $p = 7$ as the first non-maximal prime, and a clear distinction from the much rarer Wilson primes.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: A positive answer to Question 1 would show that Wilson's theorem is 'sharp' for infinitely many primes—there exist arbitrarily large primes where no shortcut to the Wilson congruence exists.

A positive answer to Question 2, combined with Question 1, would establish a striking dichotomy: for most primes, factorial residues hit $-1$ very early, but for a sparse infinite set they hold out until the last possible moment. Resolution would advance our understanding of the multiplicative structure of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and the distribution of factorial residues.
openQuestions: Are there infinitely many primes $p$ with $f(p) = p - 1$ (Wilson-maximal primes)?
Does $f(p)/p \to 0$ for a set of primes with natural density 1?
What is the density of Wilson-maximal primes among all primes—is it zero as Hardy and Subbarao conjectured, or positive as the naive random model suggests?
Can the methods used to study Wilson primes (searches to $5 \times 10^{17}$) shed light on the distribution of Wilson-maximal primes?

crossReferences.relationship: Wilson's theorem ($p \mid (p-1)!+1$ iff $p$ is prime) is the direct foundation of Problem #1072: it establishes the upper bound $f(p) \leq p-1$ and guarantees the infimum defining $f(p)$ is finite for every prime.

Immediate companion problem: #1073 asks whether composites $u$ with $u \mid n!+1$ for some $n$ are sub-polynomial in count, while #1072 studies the least such $n$ for primes. Both probe the arithmetic of factorial residues modulo primes and composites.

Direct sibling from the same Erdős–Hardy–Subbarao (2002) paper: #1074 asks about the density of EHS numbers and Pillai primes, which are defined by the same factorial congruence $n! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$ studied in #1072.

Complementary factorial-prime problem: #1058 asks which primes can divide $n!+1$ for $n$ in specific intervals, and its resolution by Luca (2001) illustrates the kind of finiteness argument that would be needed to settle #1072a.

Related modular-arithmetic problem about products of consecutive intervals modulo $p$: both #1056 and #1072 investigate when specific products (partial factorials) achieve a prescribed residue modulo a prime.

Bertrand's postulate underpins prime distribution arguments used as context for #1072: knowing that primes are 'dense enough' is relevant to understanding whether Wilson-maximal primes can be infinite or must have zero density.
